newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian govt slams Renault plant closure.
newsitem.headline: Belgian govt slams Renault plant closure.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said on Friday the Belgian government believed a decision by French car maker Renault to close its Belgian plant was unacceptable.

Dehaene told a news conference after the weekly cabinet meeting that he would take up the matter with French Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Monday. He said the two had initial talks late on Thursday, after the closure was announced.

"The government is indignant and stupefied...by a brutal decision by a head office which has taken its decision far away from the locality affected and independent of its social consequences without any consultations about alternatives," Dehaene said.
Dehaene said the government would study Belgian, European Union and OECD rules on information and consultation of employees in such instances and would consider which sanctions could be taken.

Barbara Nolan, spokeswoman for European Commissioner for Social Affairs Padraig Flynn told Reuters that under European Union law on collective redundancies and works councils companies had an obligation to inform and consult employees about their plans, as well as to inform the member state where their plants are located.
The Commission was looking at the Renault case, but had no powers itself to intervene.
"If someone feels unhappy that a law has been breached they are free to bring a case in the Belgian courts, but it is not for the Commission to prosecute companies," she said.
Dehaene later told journalists the government had been told of Renault's decision on Wednesday night.
His spokeswoman, Moniek Delvou, told Reuters Dehaene would talk to Juppe about the matter on the telephone, just as he had late on Thursday. "No meeting is planned," she said.

Belgian Labour Minister Miet Smet told Reuters that under Belgian law Renault could be fined for breaching obligations in a collective labour agreement to inform and consult employees. "The fines are calculated on a per employee basis," she said.
Recent cases had involved heavy fines, she said. She gave no examples or amounts, though.

The Renault assembly plant affected is in Vilvoorde, Dehaene's place of residence, and employs some 3,100 people. Its closure will affect at least another 1,000 people working at supply firms and subcontractors.

The Renault group is partly state-owned. The French government has 46 percent in the car maker which expects to have suffered its first loss in 10 years in 1996 because of weak markets, high costs and despite the launch of new models.
Renault said the closure was part of a wider reorganisation and would save the company 825 million French francs a year, once completed.
